question: A 55-year-old patient with acute respiratory failure is being weaned from mechanical ventilation using Synchronized Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation (SIMV). Which of the following statements about SIMV is correct?

correctAnswer: A. PEEP is contraindicated in patients with tension pneumothorax.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Applying PEEP in patients with tension pneumothorax can exacerbate the condition by increasing intrathoracic pressure and not allowing adequate ventilation.


Positive End-Expiratory Pressure (PEEP):

  • PEEP is the positive pressure that remains in the alveoli at the end of exhalation, exceeding atmospheric pressure in mechanically ventilated patients. It can be set on the ventilator (extrinsic PEEP) or may occur as a complication (auto-PEEP). (Option D)
  • Benefits of PEEP:
    • Reduces alveolar trauma.
    • Enhances oxygenation by recruiting closed alveoli, increasing gas exchange surface area.
    • Increases functional residual capacity, improving oxygenation between breaths. (Option B)
    • Improves ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) matching.
    • Increases lung compliance. (Option B)

Indications

Contraindications

  • Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): Increases FRC and improves oxygenation.
  • Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD): Reduces work of breathing by splinting airways open.
  • Pulmonary Edema: Improves lung compliance and oxygenation, especially in cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
  • Auto-PEEP: Mitigates effects of intrinsic PEEP in patients with expiratory airflow limitation.
  • Tension Pneumothorax: Can exacerbate intrathoracic pressure.
  • Hypovolemic Shock: May decrease venous return and worsen hypotension. (Option C ruled out)
  • High Intracranial Pressure: Increased intrathoracic pressure can impair cerebral perfusion.
  • Bronchopleural Fistula: May hinder healing due to increased airway pressures.
  • Acute Bronchospasm (Asthma): Can lead to hyperinflation and increased gas trapping. (Option C ruled out)



Reference:
  1. www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441904/
  2. medilib.ir/uptodate/show/1642
  3. derangedphysiology.com/files/PEEP%20indications%20precautions%20and%20contraindications.pdf

question: A patient is assessed pre-operatively for intubation by the anaesthetist and was classified on the basis of the image given below. What is the grading and the significance based on the following image?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - End tidal carbon dioxide

The image is of a waveform which represents end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2). This is a capnography waveform, a non-invasive monitoring technique used in anesthesia to measure the concentration or partial pressure of carbon dioxide (CO2) at the end of each breath.

A typical capnography waveform consists of four distinct phases:

  • Phase I (Inspiration): The baseline represents a zero CO2 level, as the patient is inhaling fresh gas without any CO2.
  • Phase II (Early Expiration): This phase shows a rapid increase in CO2 as the anatomical dead space is exhaled, mixing with alveolar gas.
  • Phase III (Alveolar Plateau): The CO2 concentration reaches a plateau as gas from the alveoli is exhaled. The end of this phase, point E, is the end-tidal CO2 value.
  • Phase IV (Inspiration): A sharp downstroke to the baseline as inspiration begins and fresh gas dilutes the CO2 in the airway.

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

Arterial oxygen saturation (SpO2) (Option A): This is measured by a pulse oximeter and is displayed as a plethysmographic waveform, not a capnogram. The SpO2 waveform is a pulsatile wave that reflects blood flow and oxygenation, not the gas exchange pattern of respiration.

Functional residual capacity (FRC) (Option C): FRC is a lung volume, the amount of air remaining in the lungs after a normal expiration. It is not measured with a waveform but through specific pulmonary function tests.

Tidal volume (VT) (Option D): Tidal volume is the amount of air inhaled or exhaled in a single breath. While the capnogram provides information about the breath cycle, the waveform itself does not directly measure the volume of air. Instead, it measures the concentration of CO2 over time, from which tidal volume can be inferred through other calculations.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A double-lumen endotracheal tube is designed with two separate lumens or channels. It allows independent ventilation of each lung during thoracic surgeries or procedures requiring lung isolation. The tube has one lumen that enters the trachea and provides ventilation to one lung, while the other lumen enters the bronchus of the opposite lung, allowing selective lung collapse and ventilation control.

[[figure-1]]

Armored endotracheal tube (Option A): An armored endotracheal tube is a specialized type of endotracheal tube that has an internal wire coil or reinforcement. This provides rigidity and prevents kinking or collapse of the tube, ensuring a patent airway. Armored tubes are typically used in situations where there is a risk of tube compression or obstruction, such as during head and neck surgery.

Ring-Adair-Elwin (RAE) tube (Option C): The Ring-Adair-Elwin tube is a type of cuffed endotracheal tube that has a preformed curvature near the distal end. This curved design helps to facilitate placement and positioning of the tube within the trachea. RAE tubes are commonly used in anesthesia and critical care settings.

[[figure-3]]

[[figure-4]]


Endotracheal tubes equipped with bronchial blockers (Option D): These are endotracheal tubes that have an additional component called a bronchial blocker. A bronchial blocker is a small balloon-tipped catheter that can be inserted through the endotracheal tube and into one of the main bronchi. It is used to selectively block the airflow to one lung while allowing ventilation of the other lung. This technique is employed for lung isolation during thoracic surgeries or procedures.

Four key Ventilator parameters:

  • Respiratory Rate (RR): Breaths per minute. Primarily affects CO2 removal (ventilation).

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In patients with blunt chest trauma, lung-protective ventilation strategies are crucial to minimize ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI).
  • One of the key components of lung-protective ventilation is limiting tidal volume.
  • The generally recommended tidal volume for patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which includes many cases of severe blunt chest trauma, is 6 ml/kg of predicted body weight (not actual body weight) to reduce the risk of barotrauma.Using 12 ml/kg will cause over-distension of fragile alveoli and sharply increases mortality in lung injury.

Lung Protective Ventilation is the current standard in mechanical ventilation which includes the following:

  • Low TV to prevent barotrauma
  • Increase RR-RR can be increased up to 30-35/min to maintain minute ventilation
  • Increase PEEP-Can increase PEEP from 4-12 even up to 16 cm H2O if needed to prevent collapse of alveoli especially in ARDS
  • FiO2 < 0.6 or 60% - If FiO2 > 60%, oxygen radical formation can occur causing worsening of symptoms

Respiratory rate - 12 breaths/min (Option A): It is within the normal range for an adult and can be an appropriate initial setting, although the specific rate may need adjustment based on the patient's condition and blood gas values.

PEEP-5 cm H2O (Option B): Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) is used to prevent alveolar collapse and improve oxygenation. A setting of 5 cm H2O is a common starting point and can be adjusted based on the patient's oxygenation status.

FiO2-100% (Option C): In the initial stages, a high fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) might be necessary to ensure adequate oxygenation, but it should be titrated down as soon as possible to the lowest level necessary to maintain adequate oxygen saturation, in order to minimize the risk of oxygen toxicity.

question: A 42-year-old man who was under home isolation after testing positive for COVID-19 develops breathing difficulty and is brought to the ER. The patient is alert and responsive but is breathing rapidly. SpO2 is measured to be 86%. He is administered oxygen via a face mask with a reservoir bag with a flow rate of 10 L/min. After a trial of one hour, his SpO2 is 88%. What is the next step in management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • End-tidal CO₂ concentration (capnography): This is the most reliable and effective method to confirm endotracheal tube placement.
  • A sustained detection of CO₂ in exhaled air indicates proper placement in the trachea and confirms ventilation. It provides immediate, continuous, and quantitative confirmation.
  • Capnography is the gold standard for confirming endotracheal tube placement during intubation due to its accuracy and real-time feedback.

Incorrect Options:

X-ray chest (Option A): Useful for confirming tube depth or ruling out complications like pneumothorax, but it is not practical for immediate verification of tube placement.

Auscultation (Option B): Helps assess ventilation by listening for bilateral breath sounds, but it is less reliable as it can miss esophageal intubation or identify asymmetrical placement.

Chest rise (Option D): A visible chest rise may indicate ventilation but does not confirm tracheal placement, as it can occur with esophageal intubation or bag-mask ventilation.



Reference:

Morgan and Mikhail’s Clinical Anesthesiology, Edition 5, Pg 127, 328, 1187

  • This mask delivers a high concentration of oxygen (60–90%) by using a one-way valve and a reservoir bag.
  • It minimizes the rebreathing of exhaled air and limits aerosol dispersion, making it suitable for respiratory infections like COVID-19.

Venturi mask (Option A): Delivers precise oxygen concentrations (24–50%) and is commonly used for COPD patients. However, it is not suitable for high oxygen demands in severe COVID-19 cases.

Hudson mask (Option B): Delivers 40–60% oxygen but lacks a reservoir bag for higher concentrations and does not effectively prevent aerosol generation.

Nebuliser (Option C): Used to administer aerosolized medications, but it can increase the risk of aerosol generation, making it less suitable for infectious respiratory conditions.

The Non-rebreathing mask is the most appropriate for patients with severe COVID-19 requiring high-flow oxygen.

    • PEEP: Use moderate levels to avoid alveolar collapse. (Option A ruled out)
    • Plateau pressure: Limit to ≤30 cm H₂O to minimize barotrauma and pneumothorax.
    • Permissive hypercapnia: Allow mild-to-moderate respiratory acidosis to avoid lung injury. (Option C ruled out)
    • FiO₂: Minimize while targeting PaO₂ >55 mmHg or SpO₂ >88%. (Option B)
  • Recruitment Strategies:
    • Use of PEEP to recruit collapsed alveoli and improve oxygenation.
    • Prone positioning: Shown to improve survival in severe ARDS (P/F ratio ≤150).
  • Advanced Techniques:
    • Neuromuscular blockade: Early use may benefit patients with severe ARDS (P/F ratio <150).
    • ECMO: Considered for severe, refractory ARDS in specialized centers.
  • Rescue Therapies (Limited evidence for survival benefit):
    • High-frequency oscillatory ventilation: No significant outcome improvements.
    • Inhaled vasodilators (iNO, prostaglandins): Transient oxygenation improvement but no long-term benefit.
  • Fluid Management:
    • Conservative fluid management: Improves oxygenation and ventilator-free days.
  • Corticosteroids: Mixed results; may benefit ARDS from bacterial sepsis but not viral pneumonia (except SARS-CoV2).

Morphine (Opioid) toxicity:

  • For a non-tolerant adult, doses of 50 mg IM can produce serious toxicity.

correctAnswer: B. Irreversible loss of all brain function, including the brainstem, with inability to breathe independently.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Brain death:

  • Brain death is defined as the complete and irreversible cessation of all functions of the brain, including the brainstem. It represents legal and clinical death, even if cardiac activity continues with mechanical ventilation.

Key features of brain death include:

1. Irreversible Loss of All Function: For a diagnosis of brain death, there must be clear evidence of an underlying cause (like a massive stroke or traumatic brain injury) that has destroyed all brain tissue. This includes:

  • The Cerebrum: Responsible for thought, memory, and consciousness.

  • The Brainstem: The "control center" for vital life functions like heart rate and blood pressure.

2. Absence of Brainstem Reflexes: In other states (like Options A or C), the brainstem might still be functioning. In brain death, all reflexes controlled by the brainstem are gone. Doctors test for:

  • Pupillary reflex: Pupils do not constrict when exposed to light.

  • Gag/Cough reflex: No response when the back of the throat or windpipe is stimulated.

  • Vestibulo-ocular reflex: The eyes do not move in response to head movement (the "doll's eyes" test).

3. Inability to Breathe Independently (Apnea): This is the "gold standard" test. Since the brainstem contains the respiratory centers that tell the body to breathe, a brain-dead person cannot take a breath on their own.

  • The Apnea Test: Doctors temporarily remove the patient from the ventilator to see if rising levels of carbon dioxide (CO2) in the blood trigger a natural breath. If no breath occurs, it confirms the brainstem has failed.



Reference:

Harrison’s principle of internal medicine, Edition 21st- Pg No. 188

question: Which of the following is true about brain death?

correctAnswer: A. Administer vasopressors to increase systolic blood pressure above 100 mmHg and wait for drug clearance before proceeding.
explanationHtml:
Answer: A) Administer vasopressors to increase systolic blood pressure above 100 mm Hg and wait for drug clearance before proceeding.

Explanation:

  • Before deciding to proceed with the diagnosis of brain death, several conditions must be evaluated and met.
  • In this scenario, the patient’s systolic blood pressure should be greater than 100 mm Hg to meet the criteria, and administering vasopressors would help stabilize the blood pressure to meet the required threshold.
  • The team must wait for five half-lives of drug clearance (adjusted for the patient's renal and hepatic function) to ensure the drugs (neuromuscular agent) have cleared, as they can interfere with the neurologic exam by paralyzing the patient, falsely mimicking brain death.

Pre-evaluation for brain death:

Several conditions must be evaluated and met before deciding to proceed with the diagnosis of brain death.

  • The cause of the coma must be identified.
  • Any confounding factors, such as severe metabolic, endocrine, or acid-base abnormalities, should be ruled out and corrected.
  • If drug intoxication or recent use of neuromuscular blocking agents is suspected, it is necessary to wait for five half-lives of drug clearance, adjusted for the patient’s kidney and liver function. (Option B & D ruled out)
  • The patient's core body temperature should be above 36°C. (Option C ruled out)
  • The systolic blood pressure must be higher than 100 mm Hg, with vasopressors administered if required.
  • A neurologic examination suggests widespread cortical destruction that is reflected by deep coma and unresponsiveness to all forms of simulations and should include testing for brainstem reflexes.


Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page No. 188
  2. Brain Death - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf (nih.gov)

correctAnswer: A. Brain death cannot be confirmed due to the presence of the cough reflex.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Brain death diagnosis requires the absence of all brainstem reflexes, including the cough reflex (mediated by the vagus nerve, CN X).
  • Since the patient exhibits a cough response, this suggests that some brainstem function is still intact.
  • Therefore, brain death cannot be confirmed.

Brain death can be confirmed as the pupils are fixed and non-reactive (Option B): The diagnosis of brain death requires the absence of all brainstem reflexes, including the cough reflex, which is still present in this case. Therefore, brain death cannot be confirmed solely based on fixed, non-reactive pupils.


Brain death can be confirmed, and the cough reflex is a false-positive result (Option C): False. The cough reflex is not a false-positive result but an actual brainstem reflex that indicates some remaining brainstem activity. The presence of this reflex means that brain death cannot be confirmed. This option is incorrect.


Cold caloric testing is unreliable in this setting (Option D): Cold caloric testing is a reliable method for assessing brainstem function. In this case, the absence of response to cold caloric testing suggests brainstem dysfunction. However, since the cough reflex is present, brain death cannot be confirmed. Hence, this option is incorrect.

Midazolam is the most commonly used benzodiazepine for conscious (moderate) sedation during short procedures such as dental procedures, endoscopy, bronchoscopy, and minor surgical interventions.

It is preferred because it provides:

  • Anxiolysis (reduces anxiety)
  • Sedation
  • Anterograde amnesia (patient has little or no memory of the procedure)
  • Mild muscle relaxation
  • Rapid onset (1-5 minutes IV) and short duration of action (30-60 minutes)

Compared with other sedatives, midazolam has a wide therapeutic index and generally causes minimal cardiovascular depression when used in appropriate doses. Respiratory depression can occur, particularly when combined with opioids, but it is less pronounced than with propofol and is reversible with flumazenil, a specific benzodiazepine antagonist.

Midazolam Conscious sedation, procedural sedation Anxiolysis, amnesia, rapid onset, reversible with flumazenil Respiratory depression (especially with opioids)

Propofol

(Option A)

Dexmedetomidine

(Option B)

Methohexital

(Option D)

 Induction of anesthesia, Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) Rapid onset Respiratory depression, hypotension

Explanation:

A fundamental requirement for day care surgery with general anesthesia is the presence of a responsible adult.

This person must transport the patient home and provide care for at least the first 24 hours post-surgery.

After general anesthesia, patients have impaired judgment, coordination, and reaction time.

The absence of a caregiver poses a significant safety risk due to the potential for:

  • Falls and other injuries.
  • Delayed reactions to medications.
  • Inability to recognize or appropriately respond to post-operative complications.

Without this support, the patient is unsuitable for discharge to their home.

Incorrect Options:

Home is 45 minutes away from the hospital (Option A): A 45-minute drive is generally considered a reasonable distance for day care surgery. The key is that the patient can return to the hospital in a timely manner if a problem arises.

The surgical procedure is expected to last slightly over 1 hour (Option B): The duration of a procedure is a factor in determining suitability for day care, but a procedure just over an hour is well within the acceptable range for many ambulatory surgical centers.

The patient has had general anesthesia in the past without complications (Option D): This is a positive factor. A history of uncomplicated anesthesia suggests the patient is less likely to have an adverse reaction to the anesthetic agents, making them a more suitable candidate for day care surgery, not less.

Explanation:

The clinical manifestations indicate malignant hyperthermia, a rare but life-threatening genetic disorder triggered by certain anesthetic agents, particularly succinylcholine. It is characterized by the rapid onset of hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, tachycardia, and metabolic acidosis following exposure to these triggering agents.

The first-line treatment and specific antidote for malignant hyperthermia is Dantrolene sodium. It works by inhibiting calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle, effectively reducing the hypermetabolic state and preventing further temperature elevation. Immediate administration of Dantrolene is crucial to prevent severe complications and mortality.

Diagnosis of malignant hyperthermia

  • Best screening test: Creatine kinase test
  • Gold Standard Diagnostic test: Halothane-Caffeine Test

Treatment for malignant hyperthermia

  1. Discontinue volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine immediately. Notify the surgeon and call for assistance.
  2. Hyperventilate the patient with 100% oxygen at a fresh flow rate of at least 10 L/min.
  3. Mix dantrolene sodium with sterile distilled water and administer 2.5 mg/kg intravenously as soon as possible. Repeat every 5 to 10 minutes until symptoms improve, with a maximum total dose of 10 mg/kg.
  4. Administer bicarbonate to address metabolic acidosis.
  5. Implement cooling measures, such as lavage, cooling blankets, and cold intravenous fluids.
  6. For severe hyperkalemia, administer dextrose (25–50 g IV) along with regular insulin (10–20 units IV for adults).
  7. Provide antiarrhythmic medications as necessary.
  8. Monitor end-tidal CO2 levels, electrolytes, blood gases, creatine kinase, serum myoglobin, core temperature, urinary output and colour, and coagulation status.

Neostigmine (Option A) is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used primarily to reverse non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockade at the end of surgery. It would treat the underlying pathophysiology of malignant hyperthermia and could potentially worsen symptoms by increasing acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions. Neostigmine is contraindicated in this scenario as it may exacerbate the hypermetabolic crisis.

Atropine (Option C) is an anticholinergic medication that blocks muscarinic receptors. It would not treat malignant hyperthermia and might actually worsen the condition by inhibiting sweating and further elevating body temperature. Additionally, it could exacerbate the tachycardia already present in this patient.

Midazolam (Option D) is a benzodiazepine with sedative, anxiolytic, and amnestic properties. While it might provide some symptomatic relief through sedation, it does not address the underlying pathophysiology of malignant hyperthermia.



Reference:
  1. Miller’s Anaesthesia, 9th Edition, Page 1118, 1123, 1124, 1125
  2. Morgan and Mikhail’s Clinical Anaesthesia, 7th Edition, Page 2301, 2302

• Subclavian venous catheterization involves inserting a needle near the apex of the lung.
  • Pneumothorax occurs when air leaks into the space between the lung and the chest wall (pleural space).
    • This can happen as a complication of subclavian line placement if the needle punctures the lung.
    • Hyperresonance on chest examination is a classic sign of pneumothorax.
    • Desaturation (low oxygen saturation) is another expected finding in pneumothorax as the lung's ability to oxygenate blood is compromised.

Central Venous Catheter Insertion:

Indications:

  • Inaccessible peripheral veins
  • Hemodialysis
  • Central Venous Pressure (CVP) measurement.
  • Administration of drugs noxious to peripheral veins

Contraindications:

  • Thrombocytopenia:
  • Coagulopathies
  • Abnormal anatomy

Complications:

  • Immediate Complications:
    • Cardiac or vascular complications (arrhythmias, arterial/venous injuries, damage to major vessels)
    • Pulmonary complications (pneumothorax, chylothorax, nerve/tracheal injury, air embolism)
  • Delayed Complications:
    • Infections (sepsis, shock, death)
    • Device dysfunction (blockage, thrombosis, fracture, stenosis, infection)

Arterial puncture (Option A): While possible during subclavian line placement, it wouldn't directly cause hyperresonance. It would typically present with pulsatile blood return and potential hematoma formation.

Cardiac tamponade (Option C): This involves fluid accumulation in the sac around the heart, which would cause muffled heart sounds, not hyperresonance.

Chylothorax(Option D): This is the presence of lymphatic fluid in the pleural space, usually due to damage to the thoracic duct. It's less likely to occur acutely during subclavian line placement and wouldn't typically cause hyperresonance.

Explanation:

  • This is the correct vertebral level corresponding to Tuffier's line. Tuffier's line is drawn between the highest points of the iliac crests, and it usually intersects the spine at the level of the fourth lumbar vertebra (L4) or the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5). It is an important reference for lumbar punctures because it helps determine the appropriate level for inserting the needle into the spinal canal without risk of damaging the spinal cord.

Incorrect Options:

L2-L3 (Option A): This vertebral level is not relevant to Tuffier's line. Tuffier's line, also known as the intercristal line, is an anatomical landmark that corresponds to the highest point of the iliac crests. It is used as a reference point for lumbar punctures (spinal taps). L2-L3 would not be the correct level for Tuffier's line.

L5-S1 (Option C): This vertebral level is not directly related to Tuffier's line. Tuffier's line is typically drawn above the level of L5-S1, as it corresponds to the highest points of the iliac crests. Lumbar punctures are usually performed below L5-S1, at the L3-L4 or L4-L5 level.

L3-L4 (Option D): This vertebral level is close to the correct answer but not exactly accurate. While Tuffier's line intersects the spine around the L4-L5 level, some sources might mention L3-L4 as an approximate reference point. However, the more precise and commonly accepted landmark is L4-L5.

explanationHtml:
Correct Option C) DC cardioversion

Explanation:

  • Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia (PSVT) is characterised by a rapid heart rhythm, which in this case is associated with low blood pressure and a weak pulse, making the situation haemodynamically unstable. Immediate intervention is essential for stabilisation.
  • DC Cardioversion: Direct current (DC) cardioversion delivers a synchronised electrical shock, which is the most effective and rapid method to terminate the tachycardia. This restores sinus rhythm, improving cardiac output and blood pressure in unstable patients.

IV adenosine (Option A): Adenosine can transiently halt the tachycardia by inducing temporary AV nodal block. However, in haemodynamically unstable patients, it is not the first choice as it may worsen the instability by causing transient asystole or severe bradycardia.

IV Diltiazem (Option B): Diltiazem slows AV nodal conduction and can terminate PSVT. However, in patients with low blood pressure and haemodynamic instability, it is contraindicated as it may further depress cardiac output and exacerbate hypotension.

Ibutilide (Option D): Ibutilide, a class III antiarrhythmic, has a slower onset of action and is not appropriate in emergencies requiring immediate restoration of rhythm. It also carries a risk of arrhythmias, such as torsades de pointes.



Reference:
  • Morgan and Mikhail’s Clinical Anaesthesia, 5th Edition, Page 483
  • Miller’s Anesthesia, 8th Edition, Page 1440

For clean-contaminated surgeries such as elective laparoscopic colectomy, prophylactic antibiotics should be administered within 60 minutes before surgical incision to ensure adequate tissue drug concentration at the time of incision.

  • Goal:
    • Achieve effective serum and tissue antibiotic levels at the time of incision
    • Reduce the risk of surgical site infections (SSIs)
  • Common organisms in colorectal surgery:
    • Gram-negative bacilli
    • Anaerobes
    • Enterococci
  • Commonly used prophylactic antibiotics:

    • Cefoxitin
    • Cefotetan
  • Timing:
    • Most antibiotics:
      • Administer within 60 minutes before incision
    • Antibiotics requiring longer infusion times:
      • Vancomycin → begin within 120 minutes before incision
      • Fluoroquinolones → begin within 120 minutes before incision
  • Redosing may be required:
    • After two drug half-lives
    • If blood loss exceeds 1500 mL
  • Most clean and clean-contaminated surgeries do not require postoperative antibiotics beyond 24 hours.

2 hours prior (Option B): Timing is early for most antibiotics; tissue levels may decline during surgery.

3 hours prior (Option C): Too early to administer the antibiotic, not recommended since it wouldn't ensure adequate tissue drug concentration at the time of incision.

Within 10 minutes prior (Option D): It may not allow adequate tissue distribution before incision.

correctAnswer: A. Stop all oral hypoglycaemic agents on the day of surgery, but stop the SGLT-2 inhibitor 24 hours before elective surgery.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

All oral hypoglycaemic agents (OHAs) should be withheld on the day of surgery, except SGLT-2 inhibitors, which require earlier discontinuation because of the risk of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).

Preoperative Management of Oral Hypoglycaemic Agents

Optimal glycaemic control during the perioperative period reduces postoperative complications. Different oral hypoglycaemic agents are associated with distinct perioperative risks.

  • All oral hypoglycaemic agents should be discontinued on the day of surgery, except SGLT-2 inhibitors, which should be stopped earlier.

  • Elective surgery: Stop 24 hours before surgery.

  • Intermediate- to high-risk surgery: Stop 72 hours before surgery to reduce the risk of SGLT-2 inhibitor-induced euglycaemic DKA.

Perioperative Risks of Oral Hypoglycaemic Agents

Drug/Class

Major Concern

Metformin

Lactic acidosis in patients with renal dysfunction

Sulfonylureas and other insulin secretagogues

Hypoglycaemia

SGLT-2 inhibitors

Euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis, especially in fasting or acutely ill patients

GLP-1 receptor agonists

Delayed gastric emptying leading to increased nausea, vomiting, and aspiration risk

Drugs to be Discontinued Before Surgery

Drug

Recommendation

Topical medications

Continue on the day of surgery

Diuretics (except thiazides)

Discontinue on the day of surgery

Oral hypoglycaemic agents (except SGLT-2 inhibitors)

Discontinue on the day of surgery

SGLT-2 inhibitors

Stop 24 hours before elective surgery; 72 hours before intermediate/high-risk surgery

Sildenafil

Discontinue on the day of surgery

NSAIDs

Stop 24 hours before surgery

Warfarin

Stop 48 hours before surgery

Short-acting insulin

Discontinue (except when administered via a continuous insulin pump)

Thienopyridines (e.g., clopidogrel, ticlopidine)

Stop 4 days before surgery (except cataract surgery without a bulbar block)

Aspirin

Stop 3 days before surgery (except in patients with prior PCI, coronary artery disease, stroke, cataract surgery, or metallic/drug-eluting stents)

MAO inhibitors

Stop 2 weeks before surgery

Continue metformin until the morning of surgery and stop the SGLT-2 inhibitor on the day of surgery (Option B): Metformin should be withheld on the day of surgery, and SGLT-2 inhibitors must be discontinued earlier (24 hours before elective surgery or 72 hours before intermediate/high-risk surgery) to reduce the risk of euglycaemic DKA.

Stop all oral hypoglycaemic agents 48 hours before surgery, including the SGLT-2 inhibitor (Option C): Routine discontinuation of all oral agents 48 hours before surgery is unnecessary. Most OHAs are discontinued only on the day of surgery, whereas SGLT-2 inhibitors follow a separate timeline depending on surgical risk.

Continue the SGLT-2 inhibitor throughout the perioperative period to reduce hyperglycaemia (Option D): Continuing SGLT-2 inhibitors perioperatively increases the risk of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis, particularly in fasting or acutely ill patients.



Reference:

  2. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1053077023008406
  3. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK540965/
